To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the United States should: (1) continue to pursue a strategy of coercive engagement, (2) use the full range of its coercive capabilities in a flexible, integrated, and balanced manner, (3) develop a more coherent and integrated national security decision-making process to support this strategy, (4) strengthen its ability to conduct effective military operations, (5) improve its ability to conduct nonmilitary operations, (6) improve the integration of military and civilian capabilities and decision making, and

(a) the use of military force is a very risky endeavor; (b) the use of force is likely to be more successful if it is part of a comprehensive diplomatic strategy that is well thought out and executed; (c) the use of coercive diplomacy is likely to be successful if the coercer can credibly threaten the target with a high cost and if the coercer is prepared to accept the risk of a high-cost response from the target.
(1) the United States should not invade Iraq; (2) the United States cannot successfully invade Iraq; and (3) even if it could, an invasion would do more harm than good.

how the dynamics of coercion affect the initiation, escalation, and termination of conflict.
the role of military force in U.S. foreign relations and with the ways in which the United States can use its military forces in the pursuit of foreign policy objectives short of war.
the dynamics of coercive military action and the limits to the use of military power.

the use of military force in international relations is an important and necessary tool in foreign policy.
the use of force, or the threat of force, is a legitimate instrument of U.S.foreign policy.

the United States has been a great power for a long time.
